new_statements.quote: P-words contrast in Chuave as to stress placement. (See Section 2.2. for features defining stress.) There are as many potential stress placements in a P-word as there are syllables. Every P-word must contain at least one stressed syllable. In describing stress patterns, V. is used to represent a syllable. All one syllable P-words are stressed when pronounced in isolation. Two syllable P-words have the following patterns: (1) V́.V. kúba 'stick'; báre 'to kick'. (2) V.V́. kubá 'bamboo type'; toró 'to cut'. (3) V́.V́. dúdí 'insane'.
new_statements.citation: Swick, Joyce. 1966. Chuave phonological hierarchy. In C. I. Frantz, M. E. Frantz, D. Oatridge, J. Oatridge, R. E. Loving, J. Swick, A. Pence, P. Staalsen, H. Boxwell & M. Boxwell, Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 5, 33-48. Pacific Linguistics A-7. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI:10.15144/PL-A7.33
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.1 'Phonological words: Contrast', p. 38 (PDF page 46 of; page 6 of the extracted Swick PDF; image); stress features sec. 2.2 p. 37; perturbation sec. 5 pp. 44-45
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (realised as high pitch plus slight intensity and lenis length, sec. 2.2) is contrastive and lexically specified: any syllable of a phonological word may be stressed, more than one syllable may be stressed (a 'multiple stress' system), and the only constraint is that every word carries at least one stress. Swick lists 3 patterns for disyllables, 7 for trisyllables and 10 for four-syllable words, with minimal pairs (kúba 'stick' vs kubá 'bamboo type'). Corroborated first-hand by the SIL Organised Phonology Data (Thurman 1992, p. 3): 'Stress is phonemic. 'birom 'his head' / bi'rom 'wild pig'; 'kupa 'stick' / ku'pa 'bamboo'. High tone almost always correlates with stress and low tone always with stressless syllable.' Tida 2006 (Dom grammar, Table 2.4) tentatively classes Chuave as a syllable-domain pitch system, consistent with this.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary distinction is drawn. Instead Swick posits multiple equal stresses per word (e.g. dúdí, nímbígá, kábúóri); a double-stressed geminate vowel cluster (e.g. gaán, oóngo) takes an extra-high pitch variant (sec. 2.2 p. 37, sec. 4.2.2 p. 42). At pause-group level one lexical stress may receive an over-riding emphatic stress as the pause-group nucleus (sec. 3.3 p. 39).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress perturbation under suffixation (sec. 5 pp. 44-45): with possessive suffixes on 2-4-syllable nouns the stem's antepenult keeps its value but ultima stress moves to the penult, and the suffix surfaces as a stressed geminate or single vowel accordingly (koba 'dish' -> na kobanaam 'my dish'); stems ending in a double-stressed geminate cluster lose the stress and final vowel and the suffix becomes double-stressed (kawií -> kawinaam); disyllabic verb stems V́.V and V.V́ both go to V́.V́ before an unstressed first-order suffix (bare -> barenangero); the suffixes -ye, -no, -ro perturb V́.V and V́.V.V stems. Pitch on-/off-glides are often lost at pause-group level (sec. 3.2). Neo-Melanesian loans are accommodated to the system (n. 5).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (P-word, 1-8 syllables); monosyllables are stressed in isolation; pitch correlates are partly neutralised in connected speech and by voice-quality registers, but intensity and length maintain the stress (sec. 4.2.1 p. 41). Based on the dialect of Gomia No. 1 village near Chuave Patrol Station; 18 months' SIL fieldwork 1960-62, main informant Waiwo (n. 2 p. 46). Thurman 1992 OPD: major villages Gomia, Mainomo.
new_statements.identity_note: Both first-hand sources describe the Chuave variety of Gomia (No. 1) village near Chuave Patrol Station / Chuave, Chimbu Province (Swick 1966 n. 2; Thurman 1992 OPD 'Major villages: Gomia, Mainomo'); this is the reference variety of chua1250 and no separate dialect glottocode applies. The OPD spells the language Chuave (Tjuave).
